lead: Software arrives as packages: archive files with a program, its libraries, documentation and install rules. A package manager is the tool that fetches those packages from a repository, a trusted server holding package metadata and files. It resolves dependencies, records installed files, and upgrades software without breaking the system. Administrators use it on every server and lab machine: install nginx, patch a kernel, remove a package cleanly. This chapter covers the Debian family (apt, dpkg) and the Red Hat family (dnf, rpm), and the difference between remove and purge.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.2 for root and sudo, plus file and directory basics from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A package is one archive file with a program, libraries, documentation, default configuration and install scripts. Debian-family systems use .deb; Red Hat-family systems use .rpm. A package file does not know the rest of the system. A package manager is the program that works with a repository: a trusted server that publishes package files and metadata, the list of names, versions, checksums and dependency rules. A dependency is another package that must be installed; nginx needs a C library and PCRE, for example. The manager downloads metadata, compares it with the local installed database, and plans one transaction. The database records every installed file and version: dpkg on Debian, rpm on Red Hat. The package list is a local copy of repository metadata, not the packages themselves. It becomes stale, so refresh it before installing. The cache holds downloaded package files; cleaning it frees disk space but leaves installed software in place. The package format is the envelope; the package manager finds, checks and records delivery. Some syllabi call this software management.
On Debian, Ubuntu and related systems, apt is the front end and dpkg is the low-level recorder. Run administrative commands with sudo.

items: sudo apt update downloads repository metadata into /var/lib/apt/lists. It does not change installed software; skipping it can make apt install use old data or fail to locate a package.
sudo apt upgrade -y installs newer versions of installed packages; -y answers yes. Plain upgrade avoids removing packages to solve conflicts; a full-upgrade may remove packages.
sudo apt install nginx fetches nginx and missing dependencies, unpacks them, runs package scripts and records the result in the dpkg database.
sudo apt remove nginx deletes program files but keeps configuration files such as /etc/nginx. sudo apt purge nginx deletes program and configuration files.

dpkg -l lists installed packages and states; ii means installed and configured. sudo dpkg -i ./tool.deb installs one local .deb but does not fetch dependencies; sudo apt install -f repairs missing dependencies. sudo apt clean clears downloaded .deb files from the cache.

sections.h3: Red Hat family: dnf and rpm

blocks.text: On Fedora, RHEL, CentOS Stream and related systems, dnf is the repository-aware manager and rpm is the low-level database tool. Repository definitions usually live in /etc/yum.repos.d.

items: sudo dnf install nginx downloads metadata, resolves dependencies, installs nginx and records every file in the rpm database.
sudo dnf update installs newer versions of installed packages. It refreshes metadata as part of the run, so a separate refresh step is often unnecessary.
sudo dnf remove nginx removes nginx and the files it owns. Dnf has no separate purge command; back up edited configuration before removal if you need it.
rpm -qa lists all installed packages. rpm -q nginx asks about one package. sudo rpm -i ./tool.rpm installs a local rpm but does not resolve dependencies; sudo dnf install ./tool.rpm does.
sudo dnf clean all deletes cached metadata and package files; the next command downloads fresh data.
Both families follow one rule: refresh metadata, then install or upgrade. The manager plans the whole set of changes; the low-level tool changes one package and leaves dependency checking to you.

examples.question: A lab machine reports 45 packages can be upgraded. The administrator runs sudo apt update, then sudo apt upgrade -y. Apt reports 12 packages upgraded and 1 newly installed kernel package not in the original 45. Next the administrator installs nginx, checks it with nginx -v, removes it with sudo apt remove nginx, then purges it with sudo apt purge nginx. (a) How many of the original 45 packages remain not upgraded? (b) How many package changes did the upgrade run make? (c) Does apt remove nginx delete /etc/nginx? Which command does?
steps: Before any command: 45 packages can be upgraded.
apt update downloads metadata; installed packages are unchanged, so 45 still await upgrade.
The upgrade run changes 12 existing packages and adds 1 kernel: 12 + 1 = 13 package changes.
Only 12 of the original 45 were upgraded, so 45 − 12 = 33 remain not upgraded. The new kernel was not in the original list.
Install, check, remove: sudo apt install nginx; nginx -v prints the nginx version; sudo apt remove nginx removes program files.
Remove keeps /etc/nginx; sudo apt purge nginx deletes program files and /etc/nginx.
examples.answer: 33 of the original 45 packages remain not upgraded, the upgrade run makes 13 package changes, and sudo apt purge nginx deletes /etc/nginx.
examples.check:
awaiting = 45
upgraded = 12
new_kernel = 1
remaining = awaiting - upgraded
changes = upgraded + new_kernel
print(remaining)
print(changes)

traps: apt update only refreshes metadata; apt upgrade changes installed packages. Running update alone fixes nothing.
remove keeps configuration; purge deletes it. The examiner often asks which one deletes /etc/nginx.
dpkg -i and rpm -i do not resolve dependencies; apt install ./file.deb or dnf install ./file.rpm do.
rpm -qa queries installed packages; it does not read a repository or install anything.
A stale package list can make apt install choose an old version or fail to find a package; refresh before install.

quiz.q: What does apt update refresh, and what does it not change?
quiz.a: It downloads repository metadata, the package lists, into /var/lib/apt/lists. It does not upgrade or install packages.

quiz.q: Why does a package manager need a repository instead of only a local package file?
quiz.a: The repository supplies current metadata and package files. The manager can then resolve dependencies, compare versions, check checksums and record one consistent transaction.

quiz.q: Write the Debian command to install nginx with its dependencies, then list installed packages.
quiz.a: sudo apt install nginx installs nginx and dependencies; dpkg -l lists installed packages and states.

quiz.q: After sudo apt remove nginx, does /etc/nginx remain? Which command deletes it?
quiz.a: Yes, apt remove keeps configuration files such as /etc/nginx. sudo apt purge nginx deletes them.

quiz.q: A server has a newer nginx available, but apt install nginx still uses old information. Explain the likely cause and fix.
quiz.a: The package lists are stale because apt update was not run. Run sudo apt update, then install or upgrade; the manager now reads current repository metadata.

quiz.q: Compare apt remove nginx and apt purge nginx for a reinstall.
quiz.a: Remove deletes program files but keeps configuration; a reinstall reuses old settings. Purge deletes program and configuration; a reinstall starts from default settings.

quiz.q: State the roles of dnf and rpm on a Red Hat-family system.
quiz.a: dnf is the repository-aware manager that resolves dependencies and installs, updates or removes packages. rpm is the low-level database and local package tool, for example rpm -qa lists installed packages.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production systems often add Snap, Flatpak or containers for application isolation, while servers still rely on apt and dnf for base packages. Configuration management tools call these managers to keep many machines identical. Supply-chain work focuses on repository signing, pinned versions and reproducible builds. Search next for apt pinning, dnf modularity and package signing keys.
